sections.heading: What are the symptoms of a stroke?
sections.body: The NHS uses the FAST test to describe the main signs of a stroke. FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999. Face weakness can make one side of the face droop, and arm weakness can stop a person keeping both arms raised. Other signs include weakness or numbness down one side of the body, blurred vision, and confusion and memory loss. Symptoms can pass quickly, but the NHS says medical help should be sought straight away even if they stop. A stroke needs urgent medical help in hospital because it can be life-threatening, so the route is to call 999. A transient ischaemic attack, or TIA, causes symptoms like those of a stroke that pass within minutes or hours. During a TIA it is not possible to tell whether it is a TIA or a full stroke, so the advice is to call 999 even if things improve.

sections.heading: What are the types of stroke?
sections.body: Most strokes are ischaemic, which means the blood supply is stopped by a blood clot. Haemorrhagic strokes happen when a weakened blood vessel supplying the brain bursts. Bleeding can be within brain tissue, which is called intracerebral, or around the surface of the brain, which is called subarachnoid. A TIA is sometimes called a mini-stroke because the symptoms are temporary. The WHO says a TIA usually lasts only a few minutes and causes no long-term damage. The CDC describes a TIA as a warning sign of a future stroke, so it needs urgent assessment. Some sources treat a TIA as separate from the main stroke types rather than as a type of stroke. Risk rises with diabetes, high blood pressure, high cholesterol and irregular heartbeats such as atrial fibrillation.

sections.heading: How is a stroke diagnosed in hospital?
sections.body: Diagnosis in hospital involves blood tests, brain scans and other tests to confirm a stroke and find its cause. Brain scans show whether a blocked artery or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke, which part of the brain is affected, and how severe it is. NHS inform says the two main types of brain scan are computerised tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The type of scan depends on the symptoms. Some people have both, and may need further scans that are good at showing the blood vessels in the brain. The Stroke Association advises that a brain scan is done soon after symptoms start. An electrocardiogram (ECG) checks the heart, and ultrasound scans can look in and around the brain. Hospitals also commonly check for diabetes and high cholesterol, and may use an ultrasound of the neck arteries called a carotid Doppler.

sections.heading: How is a stroke treated?
sections.body: Treatment depends on the type of stroke. In the first 24 hours it may include clot-dissolving medicine, surgery to remove a clot, or procedures to relieve pressure in the skull. The Stroke Association says thrombolysis uses a clot-busting medicine to break up clots and restore blood flow. Thrombectomy removes the blood clot to help reduce brain damage by restoring blood flow. It is used for people whose stroke is caused by a blockage in the large arteries of the brain. Rapid treatment is important because the benefit of thrombectomy falls over time. Clot-dissolving medicine cannot be given to everyone, for example where there are significant bleeding risks. Longer-term medicines often include anticoagulants to stop blood clots forming, medicines to lower blood pressure, and statins to lower cholesterol. The Stroke Association says most people who have an ischaemic stroke are given blood-thinning medication to help prevent clots.

sections.heading: How long does recovery take, and what does rehabilitation involve?
sections.body: The NHS says recovery time varies widely. For some people it may take days or weeks and have little impact on life. For others it can take months or years and may mean making life changes. Rehabilitation from physiotherapists, speech and occupational therapists and others is central to progress. Physiotherapy aims to restore functional movement and reduce impairment. Speech and language therapists assess and treat swallowing, speech, language and communication problems. They also assess swallowing and recommend ways to make eating and drinking as safe as possible. Rehabilitation often starts in hospital or a local clinic and may continue at home. Community stroke teams can work with people where they live. Typical teams also include dietitians, psychologists, and specialist nurses and doctors.

sections.heading: What problems can follow a stroke, and how do people cope?
sections.body: Swallowing difficulties can lead to a lung infection called pneumonia when liquid is breathed into the lungs. Poor circulation and reduced mobility can lead to deep vein thrombosis, which is a clot in a leg vein. The WHO also lists pressure ulcers, limb contracture, spasticity and shoulder pain as possible complications. Problems with language can affect speaking, understanding, reading and writing, and this is called aphasia or dysphasia. NHS inform lists depression and anxiety as common after a stroke, along with anger, frustration and sudden laughing or crying. It says tiredness can be severe and long-lasting, and can last months or even years. The Stroke Association says at least one third of stroke survivors have some form of depression within the first year. It advises that low mood can be raised with a stroke nurse or GP, and gives its helpline as 0303 3033 100.

faqs.a: FAST stands for face, arms, speech and time to call 999, the NHS says. Face weakness can make one side of the face droop, and arm weakness can stop a person keeping both arms raised. Symptoms can pass quickly, but the NHS says medical help should be sought straight away even if they stop.

faqs.q: Is a TIA the same as a stroke?
faqs.a: A TIA has symptoms like those of a stroke, but they pass within minutes or hours. It is not possible to tell during an attack whether it is a TIA or a full stroke, so the NHS advises calling 999 even if things improve. The CDC describes a TIA as a warning sign of a future stroke.

faqs.q: Which scans are used to diagnose a stroke?
faqs.a: NHS inform says the two main types of brain scan after a stroke are CT and MRI. The type of scan depends on the symptoms, and some people have both. The scans show whether a blocked artery or a burst blood vessel caused the stroke and which part of the brain is affected.

faqs.q: How long does it take to recover from a stroke?
faqs.a: The NHS says recovery time varies widely. For some people it takes days or weeks, with little impact on life. For others it can take months or years and may mean making life changes. Rehabilitation from physiotherapists, speech and occupational therapists and others is central to progress.

NHS inform lists depression and anxiety as common after a stroke, along with anger, frustration and sudden laughing or crying. The Stroke Association says depression can also appear later or return. It advises that low mood can be raised with a stroke nurse or GP.
